A_target.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \R^n$.
Then $K$ is [[Definition:Compact Space|compact]] {{iff}} $K$ is [[Definition:Closed Set (Real Analysis)|closed]] and [[Definition:Bounded Subset of Real Euclidean Space|bounded]].

B_source.statement:
Let $a, b \in \R$ with $a \le b$.
Then the [[Definition:Closed Real Interval|closed real interval]] $\closedint a b$ is [[Definition:Compact Space|compact]].

substitutions.the closed interval of the real line: a closed box in n-dimensional Euclidean space
substitutions.the one-dimensional bounded set: a bounded subset of R^n, enclosed in such a box
substitutions.compactness of the interval: compactness of the box, via finite products

derived.compactness of a product of intervals: compactness of the box, since a finite product of compact spaces is compact
derived.a closed subset of a compact set being c: compactness of any closed bounded subset of R^n

object_map.reformulation: Build the n-dimensional case as a finite product of the one-dimensional case, then pass to closed subsets.

validity_conditions: A bounded subset of R^n is contained in some closed box, which is a finite product of closed intervals.
A finite product of compact spaces is compact, so the box is compact; this is the step that carries the one-dimensional result into n dimensions.
A closed subset of a compact space is compact, giving the forward direction; the converse uses that compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed and that compactness forces boundedness.
proof_plan:
Let $K$ be closed and bounded.
Then $K \subseteq B = \closedint {-M} M^n$ for some $M > 0$.

By the source result, $\closedint {-M} M$ is compact.
By [[Tychonoff's Theorem]] for finite products, $B$ is compact.
By [[Closed Subspace of Compact Space is Compact]], $K$ is compact.

Conversely, let $K$ be compact.
The open balls $\map {B_m} 0$ cover $K$, so a finite subcover exists and $K$ is bounded.
By [[Compact Subspace of Hausdorff Space is Closed]], $K$ is closed.
Hence the [[Heine-Borel Theorem]] holds in $\R^n$.
{{qed}}
